rst31-cs2-meat-quality.title: Meat changes and species-specific quality observations
rst31-cs2-meat-quality.text: Beef cuts vary greatly in texture. The textbook links younger slaughter age in pigs than cattle with more uniform meat quality, but distinguishes fatty belly and does not guarantee the actual animal’s age/properties. Meat changes from post-slaughter rigor to ageing/softening. Select scoring, pounding or ginger-juice treatment for the purpose and dish specification. Do not age meat at room temperature in a kitchen based only on elapsed days; follow purchasing specifications and storage controls. Heat denatures proteins, causing contraction/juice loss, while collagen changes affect sinewy cuts. About 60℃ explains denaturation, not food-poisoning prevention. Quality observations include lean/fat boundaries in beef, glossy pale pink and white fat in pork, and translucent pink with skin pore texture in chicken. Combine odour, drip, elasticity and slime checks; appearance does not guarantee safety.

rst31-cs2-fish-quality.title: Seafood observation and post-processing orientation
rst31-cs2-fish-quality.text: The source’s “season” describes a fatty period, not raw-food safety approval. For whole fish check eye clarity/sinking, gill colour, belly elasticity, body firmness/gloss, odour and scales; for portions check elasticity, gloss and cut faces. The source describes seafood, especially small fish and shellfish, as deteriorating more readily than meat and calls for limiting storage-temperature variation. Three-part filleting yields two flesh sides and the central frame; five-part filleting yields four flesh portions, often from flatfish, plus the frame. Its whole-fish plating example places head left, belly downwards and Japanese accompaniments in front. Fillets face flesh forward/skin back, with Western accompaniments behind. Check store presentation standards before service.

rst31-cs2-fish-preparation.title: Check direction and position in whole-fish preparation
rst31-cs2-fish-preparation.text: Work with a stable fish using a demonstrated procedure. Scale from tail towards head, checking an application that does not damage flesh whether using a dedicated scaler or knife spine. For gills, turn the belly upwards, open the cover and detach both gill/flesh connections. Gutting incisions depend on use: open from near the gills into the belly for portions; for head-and-tail presentation, work below the pectoral fin on the reverse side to hide the incision. Rinse promptly under running water and remove moisture thoroughly. For head removal, cut diagonally from behind the pelvic-fin base towards behind the pectoral fin to the central bone, repeat on the other side and remove the head. Location diagrams do not replace practical instruction; untrained people must not begin knife work from a picture alone.

rst31-cs2-nonheat-thaw.title: Unheated-food hygiene and thawing conditions
rst31-cs2-nonheat-thaw.text: For dressed food without later heating, wash hands before single-use gloves and check that cooking chopsticks/tongs are washed. Use a clean bowl for each task and control covering/refrigeration after finishing. Raw-service frozen fish follows specified low-temperature thawing, considering tissue and drip. Some breaded semi-prepared products cook from frozen. Pre-freezing blanching is brief heat to inhibit enzymes, not completed final cooking. Do not make the textbook’s 60℃-or-above statement a universal recipe. Check labels, including frozen vegetables, for required heating versus thaw-and-eat use. Do not decide from old blanket wording that no frozen vegetables are for unheated eating or from blanching temperatures alone.

rst31-cs2-heat-equipment.title: Separate settings from actual heat-equipment conditions
rst31-cs2-heat-equipment.text: Automatic temperature control does not replace checking actual conditions with a suitable instrument. For gas equipment, inspect ventilation/burner dirt and address failed ignition or mid-operation extinguishment. Follow steam-oven opening methods that avoid hot steam, cooling/shutdown before cleaning and automatic-cleaning conditions. The 2023 textbook gives an oil-replacement example using AV 3.0, but AV is acid value, not a complete oil-safety indicator or universal legal pass/fail point. Check product, equipment and store-plan replacement criteria and do not continue with abnormal oil.

rst31-cs2-other-heat-equipment.title: Specify observations for each heat appliance
rst31-cs2-other-heat-equipment.text: Check steam production at steamer sections and water conditions/specified temperatures in noodle boilers. Near 100℃ is an example, not one setting for every model/condition. Measure griddle/braising-pan edges and centres for unevenness; learn the example of a 10℃-or-more difference but follow adjustment authority and equipment standards. Check cooked-rice quality, grill residues/uneven heat, jet-oven belts/results and tilting-kettle finished food. Do not taste items suspected spoiled or chemically contaminated; stop service and investigate.

rst31-cs2-washer-cold.title: Avoid missed checks in washers and refrigeration
rst31-cs2-washer-cold.text: Check not only washer-nozzle blockage but drain leakage, benches/racks, hot-water supply and detergent replenishment. Washing at 60–70℃ and rinsing at 80–90℃ are operating examples, not criteria for all models. Follow local equipment/chemical directions without interchanging wash and rinse. In refrigeration inspect damaged/mouldy seals, oil/dust on cooling components, food debris on removable shelves/backs and rubbish/insects in ice-making areas. Store ice scoops outside ice/bins in the designated hygienic location.

rst31-cs2-eight-knives.title: Compare eight knife uses
rst31-cs2-eight-knives.text: Long yanagiba blades slice sashimi; thick/heavy deba knives process fish. Compare vegetable nakiri for chopping/shredding with usuba for peeling/decorative work. Gyuto handles fish/vegetables as well as meat, and santoku is similarly versatile. Small petty knives suit detailed work such as peeling; Chinese cleavers use broad/heavy blades for appropriate tasks. Similar names do not justify misuse such as thin blades on hard bones. Remove moisture after washing carbon-steel knives and check residual moisture after alcohol use too. Do not arbitrarily shorten chemical contact time; dry in a way compatible with product instructions.

rst31-cs2-containers-pans.title: Care for container corners and pan materials separately
rst31-cs2-containers-pans.text: Wash kitchen pots, hotel pans, rectangular trays and bowls with suitable sponges/tools and inspect corners. Avoid metal-scourer fragments or scratching; rewash remaining dirt and apply specified disinfection. Use soft sponges/suitable detergent on fluoropolymer coatings and do not quench them hot. Dry iron pans and use manual-compatible drying heat/oil care. Pan materials include iron, stainless steel, aluminium, anodised aluminium, copper, glass and ceramics; choose for shape, thickness/depth, durability and heat-source compatibility. One scrubber/heating method does not suit every material.

rst31-cs2-historical-accidents.title: Read accident composition with a fixed year
rst31-cs2-historical-accidents.text: The 2022 chart quoted in the 2023 textbook shows falls 30%, cuts/abrasions 20%, contact with hot/cold objects 15%, reaction/overexertion 10%, falls from height 6%, collisions 5%, traffic 4%, caught-in/entanglement 4% and other 6%. Use it to practise prioritising the top three, not as current proportions or a store accident rate. Link 5S—sorting, setting in order, cleaning, maintaining cleanliness and habits—to removing objects/water/oil from routes, fixed-location storage, maintenance and repeated checks.

rst31-cs2-hazard-scenes.title: Make hazards visible by place and movement
rst31-cs2-hazard-scenes.text: For falls, inspect grating, dark routes and view-blocking loads as well as wet floors. Cuts can arise from knives, blades in sinks, can rims, broken dishes or skewers in rubbish. Use procedures preventing frozen items slipping/rolling and suitable protection for washing/waste. Burns can involve pots/oil, colleagues carrying hot items or falls on wet floors. Brewed coffee filters may retain hot water. Do not strain with heavy loads away from the body; use trolleys, divided loads or multiple people. Link picture warnings to real procedures, layout/training and heat-stress controls.

rst31-cs2-machine-guards.title: Distinguish food-machine danger zones and tasks
rst31-cs2-machine-guards.text: Cover cutting/trimming blades except where processing requires exposure, and use stopping or designated tools for hazardous loading/unloading so hands cannot reach danger. Crushers/mixers need covers preventing falls through openings and internal contact. Check guards at roller nip points and forming/pressing pinch/entanglement areas. Do not defeat lids/guards and continue. Where cleaning, lubrication, inspection, adjustment or jam removal is dangerous, normally stop and prevent restart. Check structural/legal applicability in current guidance/manuals rather than inferring exceptions from a diagram.

rst31-cs2-allergy-update.title: Distinguish the textbook’s eight allergens from current labelling rules
rst31-cs2-allergy-update.text: The 2023 textbook lists eggs, milk, wheat, buckwheat, peanuts, shrimp, crab and walnuts as the eight specified ingredients at that time. The Consumer Affairs Agency’s 1 April 2026 amendment added cashew nuts, bringing the total to nine. During the transition, do not infer absence from the label alone. Distinguish the scope of food-labelling rules from information a restaurant provides individually; check ingredients, seasonings, shared utensils and boiling water. When purchasing or recipes change, update menus, notices and staff guidance. Do not promise unverified complete elimination.

rst31-cs2-taste-complaint.title: Separate safety checks from quality improvement in taste complaints
rst31-cs2-taste-complaint.text: Do not dismiss an unusual-taste complaint as personal preference. If spoilage, foreign matter or chemical contamination is suspected, do not taste it yourself to establish safety. Stop serving the item, check ingredients, processing, storage history and the customer’s condition, and involve the person responsible. Even where routine quality tasting is safe, compare taste, quantities and processes using the store’s method. Share causes and changes with everyone involved and verify improvement during subsequent preparation or service.

rst31-cs2-workday-timeline.title: Connect work from opening through handover
rst31-cs2-workday-timeline.text: Before opening, arrange air conditioning early and check equipment start-up time, lighting/music, attendance and appearance. Starting equipment 30 minutes beforehand is an example; determine the time for actual equipment. The sample day includes service-room lights/outlets, warmers, dishes/cups, cold water, menus, frontage, seating, heating/cooling and toilets. During service replenish change, drink ingredients and supplies, clean dirty areas, and connect this with interim checks, ordering, stopping unnecessary equipment, evening preparation and handover. Balance pre-closing cleaning, replenishment and inventory with customer service and record handover information. Finally verify food, takings, fire, water, gas, equipment, entrances and security with the responsible staff. Illustrated times and change amounts belong to a particular store example, not universal operating or safety rules.

rst31-cs2-mop-window.title: Practise mop movement and window squeegeeing
rst31-cs2-mop-window.text: Spread mop strands and move backwards in overlapping figure-eights. Secure a work area without passers-by and a retreat route; practise corners and edges before the centre. The large-window example uses a suitable cleaner to wet the whole pane, then a squeegee. Wipe the blade after each pass and dry the frame last. For small windows, mirrors and areas near electrical equipment, use cloths suited to the material and specified method. Check actual product instructions rather than extending example dilution ratios, spray distances or frequencies to every product.

rst31-cs2-cleaning-zones.title: Choose tools and completion criteria by area
rst31-cs2-cleaning-zones.text: Sweep and collect exterior litter and check bin contents. Remove litter from planting areas, confirm watering for the plants/season and clean dirty lights. Distinguish waxed and unwaxed floors. Remove debris from unwaxed entrance floors, clean appropriately and wipe corners/centre with a well-wrung mop. Remove grit from waxed floors by vacuuming or equivalent and finish with specified tools/methods. Treat carpet stains according to material and chemical compatibility; use furniture wax only where material and dwell/drying conditions are confirmed. For phones and tills, confirm application to a suitable cloth rather than spraying liquid directly.

rst31-cs2-condiments-toilets.title: Keep condiment refilling separate from toilet cleaning
rst31-cs2-condiments-toilets.text: Handle remaining contents under store procedures, empty and wash containers, rinse under running water and drain thoroughly, for example inverted, before refilling. Do not merely top up dirty containers. Separate tools and contamination zones for walls, basins, outer doors, floors and toilet interiors/exteriors. Use a dedicated brush inside the bowl and specified cloth outside, never guest-area cloths or condiment-container sponges. Frequencies such as at least three daily rounds are examples; follow usage and the store plan, including tool washing/drying and handwashing afterwards.

rst31-cs2-complaint-report-items.title: Organise reports to the manager into four parts
rst31-cs2-complaint-report-items.text: Report the complaint, confirmed causes/facts, action already taken and surrounding circumstances such as nearby tables. Listen without interrupting to argue and do not assert unknown causes. The manager apologises again, explains circumstances and a proposed response, and checks the customer’s wishes. Changes of person, place or timing must respect safety and the person’s preferences. Thank the customer for raising the issue, report the response and preventive measures to head office through daily reports or equivalent, and share them to prevent recurrence among other staff/stores.

rst31-cs2-illness-training.title: Divide communication and first aid in sudden illness
rst31-cs2-illness-training.text: Check scene safety. If the person can speak, ask about symptoms/wishes and obtain necessary information from companions. However, if unresponsive, not breathing normally or uncertain, or seriously symptomatic, do not delay emergency calls for a companion’s arrival or permission. Assign the 119 call, AED retrieval, entrance guidance and other customers’ safety. If cardiac arrest is suspected, follow dispatcher instructions and received lifesaving training for chest compressions and AED preparation. If someone collapses with convulsions, avoid surrounding hazards, report the situation to emergency services and do not make independent medical judgements. Regularly practise AED location/use, calling and handover with staff on every shift.

rst31-cs2-kitchen-term-detail.title: Link kitchen terms to quantity and equipment decisions
rst31-cs2-kitchen-term-detail.text: At receiving, compare unit price, brand, freshness/ageing, damage and shortages as well as name/quantity with order conditions. Select equipment and plan temperature zones/flows from menus, ingredient processing level, cooking systems, staffing and sales forecasts. Central-kitchen processing aims at uniform taste and lower costs; specification-based ordering communicates conditions to outside suppliers even without an owned factory. Inventory ties up value as well as quantities, and prolonged storage affects quality. Physical inventory establishes quantities/value from actual goods, distinct from recorded balances.

rst31-cs2-service-term-detail.title: Use service terms as improvement indicators
rst31-cs2-service-term-detail.text: Practise cleanliness through sustained dryness, clean attractive finishes and order. CS means customer satisfaction checked through surveys/interviews, not only store self-assessment. Core products can be judged by gross-profit contribution as well as popularity; promotions also test responses to new products. Seating layouts consider party size and aisles; service stations support noticing new guests, table preparation and relaying intermediate clearing. Record what to observe and which actions to change, rather than merely listing terms/numbers.

rst31-cs2-heat-transfer-detail.title: Distinguish heating media and changes during frying
rst31-cs2-heat-transfer-detail.text: Distinguish water for boiling, seasoned liquid for simmering and water vapour for steaming. Deep-frying uses a large quantity of hot oil; food loses water and absorbs oil, so check batch loading and results. Do not treat it as the same process as stir-frying with a little oil. Follow heating conditions suited to food thickness and equipment, and do not judge internal safety from surface browning alone.

rst31-cs2-cleaning-reference-examples.title: Read cleaning-table numbers as model conditions
rst31-cs2-cleaning-reference-examples.text: The 2023 cleaning table gives examples of collecting exterior litter every 3–4 m and emptying bins at seven-tenths full. It describes daily spring/summer evening watering and once every three days otherwise, not a rule for all plants/weather. Cleaner examples include 20-fold dilution, 10 L water plus 500 mL cleaner, and spray distances of 15 cm for small windows and 10 cm for phone/till cloths. These do not establish actual-product dilution or safe distances. The furniture model leaves compatible wax overnight and wipes it next morning; toilet examples include two sprays on each cloth side and at least three daily rounds. Check dilution definitions, chemicals, materials, contact time and ventilation against actual instructions rather than acting on isolated table numbers.

rst31-cooking-service2-q001.objective: Beef texture varies by cut; select pork for use while considering differences such as belly fat. Distinguish local-breed/broiler characteristics from product specifications. Assess rigor, ageing and tenderising with storage conditions, not elapsed days alone for safety or in-house ageing suitability. Relate heat-induced contraction/juice loss and collagen changes in sinewy meat to cooking purpose. About 60℃ illustrates denaturation, not safe core heating.
rst31-cooking-service2-q001.stem: Which explanation of meat toughness is suitable for a new worker?
options: Ageing permits room-temperature storage without specified conditions
About 60℃ prevents food poisoning in every meat
Distinguish cut/sinew differences, storage changes and heating changes
All pork cuts have the same fat content
rst31-cooking-service2-q001.explanation: Assess cut differences, ageing and thermal denaturation separately.
reasons: Ageing cannot be separated from safe purchasing/storage conditions.
About 60℃ is the textbook’s denaturation example, not guaranteed pathogen control.
Assess cut differences, ageing and thermal denaturation separately.
Relative uniformity does not eliminate differences such as belly fat.

rst31-cooking-service2-q002.objective: Observe beef lean colour and lean/fat boundaries; pork’s glossy pale pink and white fat; chicken’s translucent pink and skin pore texture. Appearance alone does not guarantee safety. Common checks include off-odour, drip, elasticity and slime; keep meat in its designated storage until just before use.
rst31-cooking-service2-q002.stem: Which correctly combines textbook meat observations with their limits?
options: Cattle skin pores prove absence of parasites
More drip always means better quality in all meat
Check chicken skin texture but do not guarantee safety by appearance alone
White pork fat removes the need to check storage history
rst31-cooking-service2-q002.explanation: Observe chicken appearance and common odour/drip/elasticity signs; check safety controls separately.
reasons: Skin pore texture is a chicken observation, not a safety guarantee.
Compare drip with receiving specifications/condition; more is not universally better.
Observe chicken appearance and common odour/drip/elasticity signs; check safety controls separately.
Pork fat colour is a clue; temperature and storage history still need checking.

rst31-cooking-service2-q003.objective: Seafood season describes fatness/quality, not raw-eating suitability. For whole fish inspect eye clarity/sinking, gills, belly elasticity, body firmness/gloss, odour and scales; for portions inspect elasticity, gloss and cut faces. The source describes faster deterioration than meat, especially small fish/shellfish requiring limited temperature variation.
rst31-cooking-service2-q003.stem: Which instruction is most appropriate after receiving small fish and shellfish?
options: Weigh whole fish only; ignore eyes/gills
Serve seasonal items raw without checking temperature variation
Group everything where door opening warms it
Check item-specific quality and a storage location with little temperature variation
rst31-cooking-service2-q003.explanation: This combines quality observation and temperature control with actual specifications.
reasons: Whole-fish checks include eyes, gills, belly/body and odour.
Season describes quality timing, not raw suitability or safety.
Choose storage with deterioration and temperature variation in mind.
This combines quality observation and temperature control with actual specifications.

rst31-cooking-service2-q004.objective: Three-part filleting yields two side fillets and the central bones; five-part yields four fillets and the central bones.
rst31-cooking-service2-q004.stem: What is five-part filleting in the textbook?
options: Five equally thick cross-cut steaks
Four fillets and the central bones
Five fillets, excluding the central bones
Two side fillets and the central bones
rst31-cooking-service2-q004.explanation: Flatfish and similar fish yield four fillets plus the central bones: five parts.
reasons: A count of cross-cut steaks does not define five-part filleting.
Flatfish and similar fish yield four fillets plus the central bones: five parts.
The central bones count, so five fillets is incorrect.
Two side fillets plus the central bones describes three-part filleting.

rst31-cooking-service2-q005.objective: Distinguish textbook plating examples: whole fish head left/belly down with Japanese garnish in front; portions flesh front/skin back with Western garnish behind.
rst31-cooking-service2-q005.stem: Which matches the textbook plating example?
options: Whole fish: head left, belly down
Whole fish: head right, belly up
Portion: skin front, flesh back
Japanese whole-fish garnish always behind
rst31-cooking-service2-q005.explanation: Compare the head-left/belly-down example with store plating standards.
reasons: Compare the head-left/belly-down example with store plating standards.
The whole-fish example is head left/belly down.
The portion example places flesh in front and skin behind.
The source places Japanese whole-fish garnish in front.

rst31-cooking-service2-q006.objective: Use item-specific clues: tomato skin firmness/gloss/calyx; spinach leaf thickness, firmness, green colour and freshness; onion dry skin, firmness and sprouting; daikon leaf firmness/freshness; cucumber firmness/gloss/bumps; cabbage weight/outer leaves; carrot colour, smoothness and moderate size.
rst31-cooking-service2-q006.stem: Which matches the textbook vegetable-quality observations?
options: Choose cabbage only for lightness, ignoring outer leaves
Only long-sprouted onions count as good
Also check carrot colour and surface smoothness
Tomato calyx and skin firmness need no check
rst31-cooking-service2-q006.explanation: Use colour, surface and size as carrot-specific clues.
reasons: Observe cabbage weight and outer-leaf freshness.
Check sprouts, dry skin and firmness; sprouting is not universally good.
Use colour, surface and size as carrot-specific clues.
The tomato example includes skin firmness/gloss and calyx.

rst31-cooking-service2-q007.objective: Separate vegetables suited to cool dark storage from refrigerated ones, reduce drying/transpiration, and separate leaves/roots as needed.
options: Use item-specific conditions, limit transpiration and separate leaves/roots as needed
Wrapping only aims to eliminate every microorganism
Put all items with leaves/roots attached on one shelf
No vegetables suit cool dark storage
rst31-cooking-service2-q007.explanation: Match storage environment to item properties to manage quality.
reasons: Match storage environment to item properties to manage quality.
Wrapping controls drying/transpiration; it is not complete sterilisation.
Consider item-specific conditions and changes from attached leaves.
The source gives cool-dark examples for spring onions, onions and garlic.

rst31-cooking-service2-q008.objective: Japanese Black has native cattle/Brown Swiss and other breeding backgrounds, with blackish-brown coat examples. Japanese Brown has Korean-derived native cattle/Simmental and others, linked to Kumamoto/Kochi, with yellowish-brown examples. Japanese Shorthorn derives from Tohoku Nambu cattle/Shorthorn, mainly Iwate, with dark-brown examples. Japanese Polled derives from native cattle/Aberdeen Angus, mainly Yamaguchi, with strong black examples. Confirm actual products through delivery information.
rst31-cooking-service2-q008.stem: Which Wagyu breeding-background statement matches the source?
options: Japanese Polled is produced mainly only in Kumamoto/Kochi
The name Japanese Black makes origin records unnecessary
Japanese Brown has a strong black coat in the source
Japanese Shorthorn has Tohoku native cattle and Shorthorn backgrounds
rst31-cooking-service2-q008.explanation: Learn Japanese Shorthorn breeding background separately from its main area, Iwate.
reasons: Kumamoto/Kochi describe Japanese Brown; Yamaguchi is given for Japanese Polled.
A breed name does not automatically certify origin/product specifications.
The Japanese Brown example is yellowish brown.
Learn Japanese Shorthorn breeding background separately from its main area, Iwate.

rst31-cooking-service2-q009.objective: Scale from tail to head, applying a dedicated tool or knife spine without damaging flesh.
rst31-cooking-service2-q009.stem: A trained newcomer checks whole-fish scaling direction. Which is appropriate?
options: Open the belly then push all scales inside
Tail to head, applying the tool without damaging flesh
Head to tail, inserting the blade tip deeply
Direction does not matter; greater force is better
rst31-cooking-service2-q009.explanation: Work tail to head and compare tool application with the demonstration.
reasons: Remove scales from the surface rather than pushing them inside.
Work tail to head and compare tool application with the demonstration.
The source specifies tail to head without damaging flesh.
Check direction/tool use rather than force alone.

rst31-cooking-service2-q010.objective: Turn the belly up, open the gill cover and release the gill/flesh attachments on both sides.
rst31-cooking-service2-q010.stem: Which gill-removal location matches the source?
options: Remove only the dorsal fin without opening the gill cover
Open the gill cover and treat the gill/flesh attachments on both sides
Cut only the tail base to pull out the gills
Pull the head hard without checking one side
rst31-cooking-service2-q010.explanation: Confirm location and both-side processing in the instructor’s demonstration.
reasons: Open the gill cover and locate attachments; do not confuse the dorsal fin.
Confirm location and both-side processing in the instructor’s demonstration.
Gill attachments differ from the tail base.
Do not damage flesh or apply force without checking attachments.

rst31-cooking-service2-q011.objective: Distinguish belly opening for portions from a cut below the pectoral fin on the hidden side for head-and-tail presentation.
rst31-cooking-service2-q011.stem: For head-and-tail presentation with no visible front incision, where does the source locate gut removal?
options: Above the dorsal fin on the presentation side
Tip of the tail fin
Below the pectoral fin on the hidden side
Between the eyes
rst31-cooking-service2-q011.explanation: The head-and-tail example uses the hidden-side pectoral area, distinct from belly opening for portions.
reasons: The source does not locate gut removal above the dorsal fin.
It does not describe gut removal from the tail-fin tip.
The head-and-tail example uses the hidden-side pectoral area, distinct from belly opening for portions.
This is not a cut between the eyes.

rst31-cooking-service2-q012.objective: The head-removal cut runs diagonally from the rear pelvic-fin base behind the pectoral fin to the central bones; process the other side too.
rst31-cooking-service2-q012.stem: Before removing the head, compare the source cutting site with hands-on instruction. Which is appropriate?
options: Cut diagonally from the rear pelvic-fin base behind the pectoral fin; check the opposite side too
Cut skin on one side then tear off the rest
Cut straight from eye to mouth; no fin check needed
Scrape only the surface from tail to head
rst31-cooking-service2-q012.explanation: Confirm positions behind fins and down to the central bones; follow trained steps on both sides.
reasons: Confirm positions behind fins and down to the central bones; follow trained steps on both sides.
Forceful pulling without locating the cut is not the source procedure.
The head-removal line does not join eye and mouth.
Tail-to-head scraping describes scaling.

rst31-cooking-service2-q013.objective: Deep-frying uses abundant hot oil with water/oil exchange. Unheated mixing makes components uniform; cooling lowers temperature. Prevent secondary contamination especially where no later heating occurs. Check gloves after handwashing, washed cooking chopsticks/tongs, clean bowls each time and covered refrigerated storage.
rst31-cooking-service2-q013.stem: Deep-frying and unheated dressed dishes are taught separately. Which is appropriate?
options: Frying transfers no oil into food and changes no water content
Gloves remove the need for handwashing/tool cleaning in mixing
A bowl used for the previous task needs no fresh check
Check water/oil changes in frying and hands/tools/storage in mixing separately
rst31-cooking-service2-q013.explanation: Manage heating media/changes separately from hygiene where no later heating occurs.
reasons: Frying causes water loss and oil absorption.
Gloves do not replace handwashing or utensil hygiene.
Use clean bowls/tools for each task.
Manage heating media/changes separately from hygiene where no later heating occurs.

rst31-cooking-service2-q014.objective: Distinguish low-temperature thawing of frozen raw-use fish from semi-products cooked from frozen; follow heating requirements on each product, including vegetables.
rst31-cooking-service2-q014.stem: A frozen-vegetable box says to heat before use. Which instruction is appropriate?
options: All previously frozen items may stand at room temperature for a long time
Check actual heating requirements/methods and follow specified conditions
Bright colour permits thaw-only service regardless of labelling
Apply one old textbook sentence as the same eating method for every product
rst31-cooking-service2-q014.explanation: Follow label conditions and distinguish thaw-only products.
reasons: Freezing does not justify room-temperature holding or a universal eating method.
Follow label conditions and distinguish thaw-only products.
Appearance does not justify omitting required heating.
Check use and labelling product by product.

rst31-cooking-service2-q015.objective: Read AV 3.0 oil replacement as a 2023 textbook example, not a current safety threshold for all stores/products.
rst31-cooking-service2-q015.stem: How should the 2023 textbook’s AV 3.0 entry be used in inspection training?
options: Always continue below 3.0 despite off-odour
Record AV and core temperature as the same quantity
Call it the sole current legal safety standard for all oils
Treat it as a dated oil-change example and compare actual products/store-plan criteria
rst31-cooking-service2-q015.explanation: Teach the recorded date/conditions separately from applicable workplace criteria.
reasons: One number does not justify ignoring abnormalities and continuing.
AV concerns oil condition, distinct from core temperature.
Do not turn a textbook example into a universal current legal threshold.
Teach the recorded date/conditions separately from applicable workplace criteria.

rst31-cooking-service2-q016.objective: For noodle boilers check water/specified temperature; about 100℃ is an example. For griddles/braising pans check edge/centre unevenness; a difference of at least 10℃ is an example. Check rice quality and stop abnormal batches; grill deposits/uneven heat; jet-oven belt cleanliness/results; and tilting-kettle food completion.
rst31-cooking-service2-q016.stem: Which correctly matches heating equipment with observations?
options: A powered tilting kettle needs no food-completion check
Serve abnormal rice if orders are numerous
Check a jet oven’s belt cleanliness and finished food
Measuring only the griddle centre reveals edge differences
rst31-cooking-service2-q016.explanation: Belt deposits can affect foreign matter and heating, so inspect them.
reasons: Check cooked-food completion in tilting kettles too.
Do not serve abnormal rice; check causes and alternatives.
Belt deposits can affect foreign matter and heating, so inspect them.
Compare edges/centre to assess uneven temperature.

rst31-cooking-service2-q017.objective: Check dishwasher nozzles, drain leaks, tables, racks, hot-water supply and chemical replenishment; distinguish washing/rinsing and equipment conditions. Washing at 60–70℃ and rinsing at 80–90℃ are operating examples, not overrides of actual machine/chemical instructions.
rst31-cooking-service2-q017.stem: Which explanation of the dishwasher temperature examples is appropriate?
options: Distinguish washing 60–70℃ from rinsing 80–90℃ and prioritise actual equipment conditions
A temperature near the example permits ignoring drain leaks
All machines need no checks of water, detergent or racks beyond temperature
Washing and rinsing are the same process, so one record suffices
rst31-cooking-service2-q017.explanation: Understand numerical roles and compare specified machine/chemical conditions.
reasons: Understand numerical roles and compare specified machine/chemical conditions.
Drain leaks require inspection; temperature similarity does not justify neglect.
Nozzles, hot water, chemicals and racks also affect performance.
Washing/rinsing have different roles and conditions; do not confuse them.

rst31-cooking-service2-q018.objective: Distinguish yanagiba’s long sashimi blade; thick/heavy deba for fish; nakiri for chopping/julienning vegetables; usuba for peeling/decorative work; gyuto for meat/fish/vegetables; santoku for all three; small petty for peeling/fine tasks; and the broad, weight-using Chinese knife. Select actual specifications and trained procedures.
rst31-cooking-service2-q018.stem: Which knife-use comparison matches the source?
options: Petty has the largest blade and is only for chopping bones
Vegetable usuba should also be the first choice for hard bones
Long yanagiba is for sashimi; thick deba is for fish preparation
Gyuto cannot be used beyond meat
rst31-cooking-service2-q018.explanation: Compare length/thickness/use and select for actual specifications/training.
reasons: Petty is small and suits peeling/fine tasks.
Do not repurpose thin vegetable blades for hard bones.
Compare length/thickness/use and select for actual specifications/training.
Gyuto is also used for fish and vegetables.

rst31-cooking-service2-q019.objective: Use compatible sponges, check container corners, avoid metal-scourer fragments/scratches and reprocess residual soil. Avoid nonstick scratches/thermal shock; dry/oil iron appropriately. Select iron, stainless, aluminium, anodised aluminium, copper, glass or ceramic cookware by shape, thickness, depth, durability and heat-source compatibility.
rst31-cooking-service2-q019.stem: Which care instruction matches materials and purpose?
options: Quench every hot pot in cold water
Shiny flat surfaces make hotel-pan corner checks unnecessary
Apply iron care unchanged to glass or fluoropolymer coatings
Check container corners and select tools/drying/oiling for pot material
rst31-cooking-service2-q019.explanation: This matches tools/methods to shape and material.
reasons: Quenching may damage fluoropolymer coatings; do not make it universal.
Check corner soil and repeat washing/disinfection if necessary.
Care varies by material; do not transfer it unchanged.
This matches tools/methods to shape and material.

rst31-cooking-service2-q020.objective: Manage precision-instrument dirt, vibration and faults; always check operation after moving. Check thermometer accuracy periodically and record calibration method, results, responsible person and nonconformity action.
options: A visually clean instrument never needs accuracy checks
Separate cleaning/accuracy checks and record calibration method/results
Never check a scale’s operation after moving it
Hide the result and continue using an out-of-specification thermometer
rst31-cooking-service2-q020.explanation: Cleanliness and accuracy are separate; make methods/results/actions traceable.
reasons: A clean instrument does not necessarily measure correctly.
Cleanliness and accuracy are separate; make methods/results/actions traceable.
Check installation and operation after moving.
Report nonconformity and follow procedures such as switching to a verified instrument.

rst31-cooking-service2-q021.objective: The 2022 chart cited in the 2023 source shows falls 30%, cuts/abrasions 20%, hot/cold contact 15%, reaction/overexertion 10%, falls from height 6%, collisions 5%, traffic 4%, caught-in/entanglement 4%, other 6%. These are not current or individual-store proportions.
rst31-cooking-service2-q021.stem: Which use of the 2022 accident chart cited in the 2023 textbook is correct?
options: Use the dated composition to consider fall, cut and temperature-contact measures
Falls at 30% guarantees every store’s accident rate this month
About three-tenths overall equals an individual’s probability of falling
Small categories need no workplace inspection
rst31-cooking-service2-q021.explanation: Check chart scope/date and use it to learn observation of workplace hazards.
reasons: Check chart scope/date and use it to learn observation of workplace hazards.
Do not substitute historical composition for current/individual-store accident rates.
Category share and individual probability are different quantities.
A small share does not justify ignoring serious local hazards.

rst31-cooking-service2-q022.objective: Check grating level differences/slips; can rims/lids including pull-tabs as cut hazards; broken-dish handling and sharp waste separately. Avoid dark routes/view-blocking loads; inspect frozen-item slips/rolling, skewers in rubbish, hot coffee filters and heat stress individually.
rst31-cooking-service2-q022.stem: Beyond wet floors, which combination needs specific visual-safety checks?
options: Grating, can rims and rubbish containing broken dishes/skewers
Only wall colour and food-photo size
Exclude sink blades where guests cannot see them
Exclude pull-tab cans because cuts are impossible
rst31-cooking-service2-q022.explanation: Inspect differing fall/cut scenes concretely by place and movement.
reasons: Inspect differing fall/cut scenes concretely by place and movement.
Observe fall/cut sources as well as appearance.
Hidden sink blades can cut workers too.
Pull-tab cans still have cutting risks at rims.

rst31-cooking-service2-q023.objective: Prepare for splashing/hot oil during oil changes. Make 5S sorting, setting in order, cleaning, maintaining cleanliness and habits concrete through route clutter/water/oil removal, storage and condition maintenance. Avoid dark routes/view-blocking loads and inspect frozen-item slips/rolling, skewers in rubbish, hot coffee filters and heat stress.
options: 5S only concerns appearance, not carrying safety
Check neither protection nor task conditions for frying oil
Used coffee filters are always cold and need no check
Check oil changes, retained filter water, hot-load carrying and heat stress separately
rst31-cooking-service2-q023.explanation: Even within burn prevention, manage scene-specific hazards separately.
reasons: Removing/storing water, oil and loads also affects falls/carrying hazards.
Assess hot-oil changes and appropriate conditions/protection.
Filters may retain hot water after brewing.
Even within burn prevention, manage scene-specific hazards separately.

rst31-cooking-service2-q024.objective: Guard cutting blades not needed for processing and protect hazardous loading/unloading by stopping/designated tools. Crushers/mixers need covers preventing falls/contact; rollers need nip guards; forming/pressing machines need pinch/entanglement protection. Check current applicability and manuals.
rst31-cooking-service2-q024.stem: Which correctly matches machinery with danger-zone protection?
options: A forming machine permits reaching in while running if pinching is ignored
Check crusher/mixer covers preventing falls through openings and internal contact
Rollers cannot entangle, so guards need no consideration
Expose cutting blades especially where unnecessary for processing
rst31-cooking-service2-q024.explanation: Protect separately against falls through openings and contact with internal moving parts.
reasons: Prevent pinching/entanglement; do not improvise dangerous work.
Protect separately against falls through openings and contact with internal moving parts.
Check guards for roller entanglement zones.
Guard dangerous blade sections not needed for processing.

rst31-cooking-service2-q025.objective: Dangerous cleaning, lubrication, inspection, adjustment and jam removal normally require stopping and procedures including prevention of restart.
rst31-cooking-service2-q025.stem: What is appropriate when adjusting a jam in food machinery?
options: Skip manuals/training when rushed
Disable an obstructive cover to clean
Post a stop sign but reach in while running
Stop dangerous work and follow designated restart-prevention procedures
rst31-cooking-service2-q025.explanation: Dangerous cleaning/adjustment normally follows stopping and restart-prevention procedures.
reasons: Time pressure does not justify skipping specified safety steps.
Do not disable safety covers and continue.
A sign does not replace stopping dangerous movement.
Dangerous cleaning/adjustment normally follows stopping and restart-prevention procedures.

rst31-cooking-service2-q026.objective: Colour fixatives concern meat-product colour/flavour, exemplified by sodium nitrite/nitrate; bleaching agents whiten, exemplified by sodium sulfite/dithionite; antimould agents for citrus include ortho-phenylphenol/biphenyl; gum bases include ester gum/chicle; seasonings impart umami, including monosodium L-glutamate/disodium 5′-inosinate. Check food-specific permission/amounts separately.
rst31-cooking-service2-q026.stem: Which additive-purpose pairing matches the source?
options: Colour fixatives concern meat colour; antimould agents prevent citrus mould
Gum base is used only to prevent citrus mould
Bleaching has exactly the same purpose as meat colour fixation
Seasonings means only chemicals that whiten food
rst31-cooking-service2-q026.explanation: Distinguish purposes and separately check actual permitted uses/amounts.
reasons: Distinguish purposes and separately check actual permitted uses/amounts.
Gum base is chewing-gum base material.
Distinguish whitening from meat colour fixation.
The seasoning examples concern umami, a category distinct from bleaching agents.

rst31-cooking-service2-q027.objective: Distinguish the 2023 eight-item list from the 2026 cashew addition/nine items; missing labelling during transition does not prove absence. Check hidden sauce ingredients and shared vessels/tools; align notices/verbal guidance with current verified facts.
rst31-cooking-service2-q027.stem: How should an old eight-allergen list be used in service training?
options: Guarantee no cashews if absent from the current label
Separate the historical list from the 2026 addition and check products/shared processes
Exclude seasonings not visible in food photos
Skip all allergy checks outside those eight
rst31-cooking-service2-q027.explanation: Separate dates/current information and guide customers using verified facts.
reasons: Transition arrangements mean missing labelling alone cannot guarantee absence.
Separate dates/current information and guide customers using verified facts.
Sauces, seasonings and shared tools also require checks.
Do not bound everyone’s allergies by the list; ask what the person avoids.

rst31-cooking-service2-q028.objective: Do not taste suspected hazardous off-taste food; stop it and distinguish safe quality checks from process correction/sharing.
rst31-cooking-service2-q028.stem: A customer reports a chemical-like taste. What is the best initial response?
options: Replate without recording causes
Dismiss it as preference and continue service
Stop service, do not taste; check ingredients/process/customer condition and involve the manager
Have every worker taste a mouthful to decide safety
rst31-cooking-service2-q028.explanation: Do not taste suspected hazardous food; preserve it, establish facts and communicate.
reasons: Replating does not resolve contamination/causes.
Do not dismiss possible harm as preference without checking.
Do not taste suspected hazardous food; preserve it, establish facts and communicate.
Increasing the number eating suspect food is not a safety check.

rst31-cooking-service2-q029.objective: Opening checks include HVAC/equipment start-up, music/lights, staff/absence cover and appearance; 30 minutes is an example. Closing coordinates last orders, cash differences, held-over food, fire/security and next-day handover. Map the example to preparation, busy periods, interim replenishment/cleaning/checks, handover, pre-close and final checks, not mandatory times/change amounts.
rst31-cooking-service2-q029.stem: How should the sample daily-work diagram inform store planning?
options: Every store must use identical times/change amounts
Omit all service-time checks/replenishment because absent from the figure
Match purposes of opening, interim replenishment/cleaning/handover, pre-close and final checks to the store
Decide last orders/kitchen coordination only the next day
rst31-cooking-service2-q029.explanation: Understand each phase and plan around actual equipment, staff and required time.
reasons: Times/amounts are examples under particular conditions.
Include interim replenishment, cleaning, checks and handover.
Understand each phase and plan around actual equipment, staff and required time.
Coordinate last-order acceptance with kitchen service capacity beforehand.

rst31-cooking-service2-q030.objective: Spread mop strands, move backwards in figure-eights, secure the area/retreat and clean corners/edges and centre.
options: No retreat check is needed if guest routes are unblocked
Spread strands, overlap figure-eights and move backwards after checking area/retreat
A new mop need not clean corners/edges
Bundle strands tightly and push forward only on one spot
rst31-cooking-service2-q030.explanation: Demonstrate strands, movement/direction and check traffic/results.
reasons: Secure safety of people working and your retreat route.
Demonstrate strands, movement/direction and check traffic/results.
Corners/edges are also within the cleaning area.
The source example moves spread strands.

rst31-cooking-service2-q031.objective: For large panes use suitable cleaner, wet the whole surface, squeegee, wipe the blade each time and dry the frame.
rst31-cooking-service2-q031.stem: Which large-window squeegeeing method matches the source?
options: Every other cleaner must use the same dilution
Never wipe a dirty squeegee until all windows are finished
Wet all, squeegee, wipe tools each time and dry the frame
Wet only part and always leave the frame wet
rst31-cooking-service2-q031.explanation: Check wetting, water removal, tool wiping and frame drying.
reasons: Compare dilution/use with actual instructions.
Wiping after each pass affects the finish.
Check wetting, water removal, tool wiping and frame drying.
Distinguish whole-pane treatment from final frame drying.

rst31-cooking-service2-q032.objective: Unwaxed entrance floors: remove debris, clean compatibly, use a well-wrung mop at corners/centre. Waxed floors: remove grit, finish with specified tools/methods. Treat carpet stains compatibly; wipe furniture and wax only suitable materials under specified drying conditions. Apply cleaner to suitable cloths for phones/tills, not directly.
rst31-cooking-service2-q032.stem: Which cleaning approach fits place and material?
options: Spray phones/tills heavily so liquid enters
Use every chemical identically on carpet stains
Every furniture item must use the example wax
Distinguish wax/material and check chemical/tool conditions
rst31-cooking-service2-q032.explanation: Suitable methods vary with floor/furniture material and surface treatment.
reasons: Avoid liquid entry and check specified cloth methods.
Check compatibility among stain, material and chemical.
Use wax only with confirmed compatible materials/product conditions.
Suitable methods vary with floor/furniture material and surface treatment.

rst31-cooking-service2-q033.objective: Condiment containers: handle contents, wash, rinse, drain, refill. Separate toilet wall/basin/door and floor tools; use dedicated internal brushes/flush and external tools. Concentrations, spray distances, seasonal watering and round counts are examples; set methods/frequencies for instructions/materials/store plans.
rst31-cooking-service2-q033.stem: Which instruction manages refilling and toilet cleaning?
options: Check contents handling, washing, rinsing, draining/refilling; separate toilet tools
Top up without washing even with contents remaining
Never reconsider usage after setting an example frequency
Rinse a toilet brush and immediately use it for condiment containers
rst31-cooking-service2-q033.explanation: Manage food-contact container steps separately from toilet contamination zones.
reasons: Manage food-contact container steps separately from toilet contamination zones.
Topping up dirty containers is not completed cleaning.
Compare example frequency with store usage/plans.
Do not repurpose toilet tools for food containers.

rst31-cooking-service2-q034.objective: Complaint handling includes apology, uninterrupted listening, concrete initial action, manager re-apology/explanation/proposal/wishes check, thanks and head-office reporting. Distinguish complaint, verified facts/causes, completed action and nearby circumstances; share preventive measures.
rst31-cooking-service2-q034.stem: What information is needed when handing a complaint to the manager?
options: Only personality inferred from appearance
Only the worker’s wish to refund
Only an assumed conclusion despite unverified causes
Complaint, verified facts, completed action and surroundings
rst31-cooking-service2-q034.explanation: Provide information for management judgement without making the customer repeat everything.
reasons: Inferred personality does not convey facts/response history.
Organise the customer’s complaint/facts/actions, not worker preferences.
Passing unverified causes as conclusions can misdirect the response.
Provide information for management judgement without making the customer repeat everything.

rst31-cooking-service2-q035.objective: Obtain necessary information from the person/companion but do not delay 119 for wishes confirmation in abnormal responsiveness/breathing. In suspected convulsions/cardiac arrest, assign safety/calling/AED roles, follow dispatcher/trained procedures and practise regularly.
rst31-cooking-service2-q035.stem: A customer is unresponsive and you are unsure whether breathing is normal. What is appropriate?
options: Everyone gathers without entrance guidance
Assign 119/AED roles and follow dispatcher/trained procedures
Give water then wait a long time for recovery
Wait for companions before calling or arranging AED
rst31-cooking-service2-q035.explanation: Proceed with emergency help and follow current lifesaving training/dispatcher instructions.
reasons: Divide calling, first aid, entrance guidance and other guests’ safety.
Proceed with emergency help and follow current lifesaving training/dispatcher instructions.
Do not independently give food/drink to an unresponsive person.
Do not delay emergency calls for companions when responsiveness/breathing is abnormal.

rst31-cooking-service2-q036.objective: In suspected convulsions/cardiac arrest, assign safety/calling/AED roles, follow dispatcher/trained procedures and practise regularly.
rst31-cooking-service2-q036.stem: Which store training for a customer collapsing with convulsions is appropriate?
options: Avoid surrounding hazards and practise emergency reporting/guidance roles
Train once only and do not inform night staff
Only the manager needs to know the AED location
Staff decide the diagnosis and do not call without companions
rst31-cooking-service2-q036.explanation: Avoid independent medical judgement; practise calling, safety and handover roles.
reasons: Avoid independent medical judgement; practise calling, safety and handover roles.
Train regularly, including replacement staff.
Sudden illness can occur at any hour; staff need locations/contact methods.
Do not assert diagnoses or prevent necessary calls.
